The Spread

The Story of Islam

The Spread

Islam Across the World

In plain English — the journey that carried Islam across the world, and the unity that held so many peoples together

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with a harbour in the morning, sailing boats, a desert road, the blue domes of Samarkand, the mud mosque of Timbuktu, and the red-and-white arches of Cordoba.

The story is told plainly — the meaning of tradition's words is given in our own English, not as word-for-word quotation. Where a line is quoted directly, the book says plainly that this is what tradition says.

At the end of every part, a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story these questions matter as much as the story itself — because this story is about how one faith reached so many different peoples.

There are two kinds of things in this book — the evidence of history, such as old mosques, the ruins of ports, books written by travellers, and books written by scholars; and the stories of tradition, which have been told for centuries in the books of al-Tabari, al-Masudi and Ibn Battuta. Where the story is tradition's, the book says so plainly — 'tradition says'. Where something rests on evidence, the book names it.

One thing must be said first — Islam did not spread by the sword alone. It went in merchants' ships, on the feet of Sufis along desert roads, and in the books of scholars. This book tells that journey — and where there was fighting, the book does not hide it, but it does not make fighting the whole story.

There is no picture of the Prophet Muhammad in this book — not as a grown man, not as a child, not as an infant, not in shadow, not from behind. And there is no recognisable picture of any well-known man either. The pictures in this book show only ports, mosques, trade routes, libraries, gardens and deserts — no people at all.

The main story of this book is from al-Tabari's History, al-Masudi's Meadows of Gold, Ibn Battuta's Rihla, and modern scholars. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

No date in this book is taken as settled — where dates differ, the book says so in a separate note. Where there are two views, both are recorded in their own notes — and the book has not decided between them.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

The traders — Arab, Persian, Gujarati and Chinese merchants, who carried spices, silk, gold and cloth along the sea and desert roads — and carried their faith with them too.

The Sufis — the dervishes and saints who lived in lodges, spoke of love of God, and at whose doors Hindu and Muslim alike came — like Muinuddin Chishti of Ajmer and Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi.

The scholars — al-Bukhari of Bukhara, al-Tabari of Baghdad, Rumi of Balkh, and hundreds of names whose books were read from Baghdad to Samarkand, from Delhi to Timbuktu.

Mansa Musa (about 1312–1337) — king of Mali; he went on hajj in 1324, and the story of his gold is still told today.

Ibn Battuta (1304–1369) — traveller from Morocco; from about 1325 to 1354 he journeyed from Morocco to China, and wrote the book of his travels, the Rihla.

Zheng He (1371–1433) — Chinese Muslim admiral; with the Ming emperor's great fleet he made seven sea voyages from 1405 to 1433, and reached East Africa.

The Wali Songo — the nine saints of Java, of whom tradition says they spread Islam in Java.

Tariq ibn Ziyad (about 711) — the commander of whom tradition says he set foot in Spain in 711 — and from whose name Gibraltar takes its name.

1 · How Islam Travelled — Not Only by Conquest, but by Trade, by Sufis, by Scholars · · HOW ISLAM TRAVELLED — NOT ONLY BY CONQUEST, BUT BY TRADE, BY SUFIS, BY SCHOLARS

In the seventh century, Islam set out from Arabia — and within three hundred years it had spread from Spain to India. But this spread did not happen in one way only. In some places armies went — but in many places no army ever went at all. There Islam went in a trader's ship, on a Sufi's feet, and in a scholar's book.

First, understand trade. Arab traders had sailed the sea routes since the Prophet's own time — from Yemen to India, from India to Southeast Asia, and to the coast of East Africa. When they became Muslim, they began to carry their faith with them too — not by showing anyone a sword, but by living there, marrying there, and trading honestly. Mosques were built in the ports — and the people of the ports slowly began to pray with them.

Then came the Sufis. Sufis were people who spoke of love of God and of cleansing the heart. They lived in lodges — where anyone could come, rich or poor, Muslim or not. They sang poetry, helped people, and prayed for the sick. Their words touched people's hearts — and people came to them, without any pressure. In India, in Central Asia, in Africa and in Southeast Asia — everywhere, the Sufis' way was the same.

Then came the scholars — and books came. Arabic became the language in which scholars from Spain to India could understand one another. The books of Baghdad were read in Samarkand, the books of Samarkand were read in Delhi, and the books of Delhi were read in Timbuktu. One Quran, one language, and one learning — that was the thread that bound so many different peoples together.

And yes — there was fighting too. Armies went into Persia, Syria, Egypt and Spain, cities fell, and governments changed. This book does not hide that — where there was fighting, the book says so. But this book says one thing plainly — fighting changed governments, but the work of changing hearts was most often done by traders, Sufis and scholars. Modern scholars, like Richard Bulliet, say that even in Persia it took two or three hundred years for Islam to become the majority — a sword does not change hearts in a single day.

The three roads of the spread — what modern scholars say

That Islam spread along the roads of trade, of the Sufis and of the scholars — this is what modern scholars say, such as Marshall Hodgson (The Venture of Islam), Ira Lapidus (A History of Islamic Societies) and Thomas Arnold (The Preaching of Islam). Thomas Arnold's book is on this very question — that Islam spread not by the sword, but by preaching. In this book, fighting is not hidden — but it is not made the whole story.

Two or three hundred years for a majority in Persia — Bulliet's count

That it took two or three hundred years for Muslims to become the majority in Persia — this is what Richard Bulliet (Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period) says — he reached this estimate by counting old names and family lines. Modern scholars say this count is an estimate, not a firm figure — but it is certain that the change happened slowly, not in a single day.

Pause and think — If Islam had spread only by the sword, how would it have reached the places where no army ever went — like Indonesia, or China, or the Swahili coast? Is the strongest way to spread a faith to let people see it lived — rather than to show them a sword?

2 · Persia — The Conversion, the Scholars, the Poets · · PERSIA — THE CONVERSION, THE SCHOLARS, THE POETS

Persia — today's Iran — was the first great empire to come within the fold of Islam. In the seventh century Arab armies defeated the Sasanian empire — but the hearts of the people of Persia did not change in a single day. Tradition says that at first only a few people became Muslim — the traders of the cities, the people of the court — and in the villages people stayed with their old faith.

Persia had old faiths — the Zoroastrian faith, which was the faith of the Sasanian kings; the Christian faith, which had been in the cities of Persia for centuries; and the Jewish faith too. After Islam came, these faiths did not end — Zoroastrians, Christians and Jews went on living in Persia, with their temples and churches. But slowly, generation by generation, more people became Muslim — and by the tenth century Muslims were the majority in Persia.

Persia did not only take Islam — it also gave Islam its own language and its own poetry. The Persian language did not die — it became the second great language of Islam. The Quran was read in Arabic, but poetry was written in Persian — and that poetry is still sung all over the world today.

You have already heard the names of Persia's scholars in the last book — al-Tabari, whose History is a source for this book too, was from Persia; al-Bukhari, whose book of hadith is the most honoured, was from Bukhara; al-Ghazali, who wrote on faith and philosophy, was from Tus. And among the poets, Rumi — who was born in Balkh and lived in Konya — his Masnavi is still read today. Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnameh — the story of the old kings of Persia — which is a story from before Islam, but written in the Persian language.

One more thing — in Persia, Islam also took on a colour of its own. Later, in the sixteenth century, in the time of the Safavid kings, Shia Islam became strong in Persia — but that story is not this book's; it belongs to a later time. In this book, remember only this — in Persia, Islam spread slowly, generation by generation — and the Persian language and poetry gave Islam a new voice.

The change in Persia was slow — what Bulliet and Hodgson say

That it took two or three hundred years for Muslims to become the majority in Persia — this is what Richard Bulliet (Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period) says. Marshall Hodgson (The Venture of Islam) says that the Persian language and culture gave Islam a new form — Arabic stayed the language of the Quran, but Persian became the language of poetry and of the court.

Ferdowsi's Shahnameh — a story from before Islam, in the Persian language

Ferdowsi's Shahnameh is the story of the old kings of Persia — from before Islam — but it was written in the Persian language, after Islam came. In this book it is not called an Islamic book — it is a story of the Persian language.

Pause and think — The people of Persia changed their faith — but they did not change their language. Does taking up a new faith mean giving up your old language and poetry — or can a new thing be said in your own language?

3 · Central Asia — Samarkand, Bukhara, and the Silk Road · · CENTRAL ASIA — SAMARKAND, BUKHARA, AND THE SILK ROAD

Beyond Persia lay Central Asia — today's Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Tajikistan — the land through which the Silk Road passed. Silk came from China, cloth from Persia, spices from India — and all of it passed through the markets of Samarkand and Bukhara.

Samarkand — the city of which it was said that it was one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Tradition says that paper-making also began in Samarkand — learned from craftsmen from China. That after the Battle of Talas in 751 the craft was learned from Chinese prisoners — this is a story of tradition, and modern scholars say that paper came slowly, not from a single battle.

Bukhara — the city of scholars. Al-Bukhari (810–870) was born here — his book of hadith, the Sahih al-Bukhari, is today the most honoured among Sunni Muslims. Ibn Sina (980–1037) was born near here — you read in the last book about his book of medicine, the Canon. And al-Khwarizmi — whose numerals we still count with today — was from Khwarazm, which lies here in Central Asia.

In Central Asia too, Islam spread along the roads of traders and Sufis. Tradition says that the traders of Samarkand went among the Turkic tribes — and Islam went with them. The Turkic tribes slowly became Muslim — first their chiefs, then their people. And from those very Turks came the Seljuks — of whom you read in the last book — and later the Ottomans too, whose story will come in later books.

In the cities of Central Asia, madrasas were built — where children read the Quran, and great scholars taught law, mathematics and astronomy. The Registan madrasa of Samarkand still stands today — with its blue domes — and it tells us that this city was not only a market, it was also a city of learning.

Talas 751 and paper — a story of tradition

That after the Battle of Talas in 751 the craft of paper-making was learned in Samarkand from Chinese prisoners — this is a story of tradition, from sources after al-Tabari's History. Modern scholars say that paper came to Central Asia slowly — and in this book 751 is not taken as a settled date.

Al-Bukhari and Ibn Sina — the names and the places

That al-Bukhari was born in Bukhara (810) and Ibn Sina was born near Bukhara (980) — this comes from Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist and from modern scholars such as Marshall Hodgson. That al-Khwarizmi was from Khwarazm comes from there too.

Pause and think — In Samarkand, silk was sold, and books were also read — in the same city. Do trade and learning travel together — or should one stay apart from the other? And does a city become great only from its market — or from its madrasa too?

4 · India — The Delhi Sultanate, the Sufis, and the Mughals in Brief · · INDIA — THE DELHI SULTANATE, THE SUFIS, AND THE MUGHALS IN BRIEF

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it tells of battles and of cities falling, in a line or two, without any detail.

Islam came to India by two roads — by sea, and by land. By sea came the traders — Arab ships had come to the Malabar coast since the Prophet's own time. Tradition says that the king of Kerala, Cheraman Perumal, became Muslim — this is a story of tradition, and modern scholars say there is no firm evidence for it — but Muslim traders on the Malabar coast are truly very old.

By land, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim came to Sindh in 711 — tradition gives this date. Then for centuries there were battles in the north-west of India — and in 1206 Qutb-ud-din Aibak founded a sultanate in Delhi — the beginning of the Delhi Sultanate. In this book no detail of the fighting is given — only that it happened, and a new government was formed in Delhi.

But the Delhi Sultanate is not only a story of fighting — it is also a story of Sufis. In the time of the Sultanate, the lodges of the Sufis spread across India — and Hindu and Muslim alike came to their doors. Muinuddin Chishti (about 1142–1236) lived in Ajmer — his shrine is to this day a place of faith for Hindu and Muslim alike. Nizamuddin Auliya (1238–1325) lived in Delhi — and his disciple Amir Khusrau (1253–1325) wrote poetry in Persian and in Hindavi — both.

Alongside the Sufis, there was also a wave of bhakti in India — Kabir, Nanak and other saints, who spoke of one God, of cleansing the heart, and of humanity. Modern scholars, like Richard Eaton, say that in India Islam spread more through Sufis and traders than through the sword — and in regions like Bengal no army ever went at all, yet people became Muslim there — farmers, weavers, fishermen — slowly, generation by generation.

And the Mughals? Their story here is only a bridge — in 1526 Babur defeated the Delhi Sultanate at the Battle of Panipat, and the Mughal empire began. Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb — their full story is the next book's. In this book, remember only this — when Islam came to India, it became India's own — Hindavi joined its poetry, Indian spices joined its food, and Hindu and Muslim alike began to come to its shrines.

Cheraman Perumal — a story of tradition, no firm evidence

The story that Cheraman Perumal, the king of Kerala, became Muslim — this is a story of tradition. Modern scholars, like Richard Eaton, say there is no firm evidence for it — but that Arab Muslim traders on the Malabar coast are very old rests on evidence.

The spread in Bengal — not by the army, but by Sufis

That Islam spread in Bengal not by the army — this is what the modern scholar Richard Eaton (The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier) says — there, farmers and weavers slowly became Muslim, along the road of the Sufis. In this book Bengal is not called a story of the sword.

Pause and think — Hindu and Muslim alike come to the shrine of Ajmer — for centuries. Should the door of a shrine or a temple be only for the people of one faith — or can anyone come who comes with a true heart?

5 · Southeast Asia — The Traders, the Ports, and the Wali Songo · · SOUTHEAST ASIA — THE TRADERS, THE PORTS, AND THE WALI SONGO

Southeast Asia — today's Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines — is the place where Islam spread without any army. No Arab army ever came here — yet today Indonesia is the largest Muslim country in the world. How did this happen?

The answer is — the traders. Traders from Gujarat, Arabia and Persia had come for centuries to the ports of Malacca, Aceh and Java — to take spices, and to sell cloth. They lived in the ports, married there, and built mosques there. The kings of the ports began to join with them — because friendship with traders meant wealth and ships. Between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, one by one, the kings of the ports became Muslim — and their people with them.

In Java, the story of Islam is joined to the Wali Songo — the nine saints. Tradition says that these nine saints came to Java — they taught people Islam, built mosques, and joined Java's own arts — wayang (shadow puppetry) and gamelan (music) — with Islam. That the Wali Songo were truly nine, and what each of them did — this is a story of tradition, and modern scholars say there is little firm evidence about them — but that Islam spread in Java along the road of the Sufis, that is certain.

In Southeast Asia, Islam took on a colour of its own — mosques here were built with roofs like those of China, or like those of Java — tall, pointed roofs. The Malay language joined its poetry, and the old customs of the land stayed in its festivals too. Modern scholars say — in Southeast Asia, Islam did not arrive, it was taken up — kings took it up because it was a road to trade, to learning, and to the world.

The Wali Songo — a story of tradition

The story of the nine saints of Java — the Wali Songo — is a story of tradition, from Java's own books. Modern scholars say there is little firm evidence about the names and deeds of the nine saints — but that Islam spread in Java along the road of Sufis and traders is certain, from Ibn Battuta's Rihla and modern scholars such as Ira Lapidus.

The kings of the ports becoming Muslim — joined to trade

That the kings of Malacca and Aceh became Muslim — between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries — comes from Ibn Battuta's Rihla and modern scholars such as Marshall Hodgson. That they took up Islam because of trade — this is the view of modern scholars, not firm evidence — and in this book it is recorded as a view.

Pause and think — No army came to Indonesia — yet it has the most Muslims of any country. Does this mean that the strongest way to spread a faith is not the sword, but trade, friendship and the words of Sufis?

6 · China — The Hui, and the Mosques of Xi'an and Quanzhou · · CHINA — THE HUI, AND THE MOSQUES OF XI'AN AND QUANZHOU

Islam came to China with the traders — in the time of the Tang dynasty, in the seventh and eighth centuries, Arab and Persian traders began to come to the ports of China. Tradition says that the Prophet's Companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas went to China — this is a story of tradition, and modern scholars say there is no firm evidence for it. But that Muslim traders were in China is very old — their mosques at the port of Quanzhou date from the eighth century.

One of the most famous mosques of China is the Great Mosque of Xi'an. Tradition says it was built in 742 — this is a date of tradition, and the building that stands today was built in later centuries. But the most special thing about this mosque is this — it looks Chinese. Its roofs are Chinese, its gardens are Chinese, and its minaret is like a Chinese tower — only in the decoration inside is there a glimpse of Islam.

The Muslims of China are called the Hui — people who have lived in China for centuries, speak Chinese, eat Chinese food, and are Muslim. Hui people are in every part of China — and their mosques look Chinese too. Islam did not force its own shape on China — it took a Chinese shape.

And from China comes a name that is the greatest name of this book's journey — Zheng He (1371–1433). Zheng He was a Chinese Muslim admiral — commander of the Ming emperor's great fleet. Between 1405 and 1433 he made seven sea voyages — to Southeast Asia, India, Persia, Arabia, and East Africa. Tradition says his ships were the largest ships of that time — and that thousands of people sailed in his fleet. Zheng He was Muslim — and when he went to Mecca, he also performed the hajj.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas going to China — a story of tradition

That the Prophet's Companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas went to China — this is a story of tradition, from the books of China's own Muslims. Modern scholars say there is no firm evidence for it — but that Muslim traders were in Quanzhou from the eighth century rests on evidence.

The Xi'an mosque, 742 — a date of tradition

That the Great Mosque of Xi'an was built in 742 — this is a date of tradition. The building that stands today is from later centuries — this is what modern scholars say. In this book 742 is not taken as a settled date.

Zheng He's seven voyages, 1405–1433

Zheng He's seven sea voyages (1405–1433) and his reaching East Africa — this comes from the history of the Ming dynasty and modern scholars such as Marshall Hodgson. The count of the size of his ships is tradition's — and modern scholars say the counts differ.

Pause and think — The mosque of Xi'an looks Chinese — its roofs are Chinese, its garden is Chinese. Should a mosque look the same everywhere — or can it take the shape of the place where it is built? And is a faith known by the shape of its building — or by what is inside?

7 · Africa — The Swahili Coast, West Africa, Timbuktu, and Mansa Musa's Hajj · · AFRICA — THE SWAHILI COAST, WEST AFRICA, TIMBUKTU, AND MANSA MUSA'S HAJJ

Islam came to Africa from two sides — from the eastern coast, and across the western desert. The eastern coast — the Swahili coast — was the place where Arab and Persian traders had come for centuries — to take gold, ivory and spices. Mosques were built in the ports of Kilwa, Lamu and Mombasa — and the people there slowly became Muslim.

One of the most famous buildings of the Swahili coast is the Great Mosque of Kilwa, which was built of coral stone. Tradition says that the kings of the Swahili coast came from Arabia — this is a story of tradition, and modern scholars say that the Swahili people were truly of Africa itself — they took Islam from Arab traders, they did not come from Arabia. Arabic words joined the Swahili language — but it stayed a language of Africa.

In West Africa, Islam came across the Sahara desert — traders carried gold and salt on camels, and Islam went with them. The kings of the empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhai slowly became Muslim — and scholars began to come to their courts.

The most famous name of West Africa is Mansa Musa (about 1312–1337), king of Mali. In 1324 he went on hajj — towards Mecca, with thousands of people, and carrying gold. Tradition says — and it is recorded in the book of al-Umari — that when he passed through Cairo, he gave away so much gold that the price of gold in Cairo itself fell. Whether the price of gold truly fell, and for how many years it stayed low — this is a story of the sources, and modern scholars say it is greatly exaggerated — but it is certain that Mansa Musa's hajj was very great, and that after it the name of Mali spread far and wide.

After Mali came Timbuktu — the city that became a city of learning in the middle of the desert. There were the Sankore mosque and madrasa — where thousands of students studied. Tradition says that in Timbuktu there were thousands of books — and old manuscripts are still found there today. The sixteenth-century scholar Ahmed Baba was from Timbuktu — his books are still read today.

In Africa too, Islam spread along the roads of traders and scholars — not by the army. And Africa also gave Islam its own voice — Swahili poetry, the scholars of Mali, and the books of Timbuktu — all of these became part of the world of Islam.

The Swahili kings coming from Arabia — a story of tradition

That the kings of the Swahili coast came from Arabia — this is a story of tradition, from the Swahili's own books. Modern scholars say that the Swahili people were of Africa itself — they took Islam from Arab traders. The ruins of the Great Mosque of Kilwa are evidence from archaeology.

Mansa Musa's gold — a story of the sources, greatly exaggerated

The story of Mansa Musa's hajj (1324), of gold given away in Cairo, and of the price of gold falling — this comes from the book of al-Umari, which was written only a few years after Mansa Musa. Modern scholars say the story of the price of gold falling is greatly exaggerated — but the greatness of the hajj and the spreading of Mali's name are certain. In this book no count is taken as settled.

Pause and think — Timbuktu lay in the middle of the desert — yet there were thousands of books there. Does learning need great cities — or can a city of learning stand in the middle of a desert too? And why is the story of Mansa Musa's gold still told today — because of the gold, or because of the hajj?

8 · Spain and Sicily — al-Andalus, Living Together, and the Fall of Granada (1492) · · SPAIN AND SICILY — AL-ANDALUS, LIVING TOGETHER, AND THE FALL OF GRANADA (1492)

711. Tradition says that Tariq ibn Ziyad landed in Spain — near Gibraltar — and Gibraltar takes its name from him — Jabal al-Tariq, the mountain of Tariq. Within a few years, a large part of Spain had come under Muslim rule — and that part was called al-Andalus.

The capital of al-Andalus was Cordoba. In the tenth century Cordoba was one of the largest cities in the world — tradition says that millions of people lived there, and that there were thousands of mosques. The Great Mosque of Cordoba — the Mezquita — still stands today — its red-and-white arches are famous all over the world.

One thing is often said about al-Andalus — convivencia, living together — that Muslims, Christians and Jews lived together, read one another's books, and learned from one another. This is true, and also not fully true. It is true that in Cordoba, Muslim, Christian and Jewish scholars worked together — Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), whom Europe calls Averroes, and Maimonides (1138–1204), the Jewish philosopher, were both from Cordoba.

But living together also had limits. Christians and Jews were dhimmis — that is, they were allowed to keep their faith, but they had to pay the jizya, and they did not have the same standing as Muslims. And in some times — above all in the time of the Almohads — there was harshness against Christians and Jews — Maimonides himself had to flee Cordoba. In this book both things are recorded together — the living together, and its limits.

In Sicily the story was the same — Muslim rule, and Christians and Jews living alongside — but in Sicily Muslim rule had already ended in the eleventh century — the Norman kings took it.

◆ ◆ This part is not for younger listeners — it tells of a city falling and of people being driven out, in a line or two, without any detail.

1492. The last Muslim city of Spain — Granada — laid down its arms. The Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada — and the story of al-Andalus, nearly eight hundred years long, came to an end. In this book no detail of the fighting is given — only that it happened, and Granada fell.

What happened after the fall of Granada must also be told — in 1492 itself the Jews of Spain were ordered to leave the country — and later the Muslims too — first they were told to become Christian, and then in 1609 they too were driven out of the country. This is told plainly — because it is part of the story, and hiding it would be wrong.

Convivencia — a golden age, and limits too

Convivencia — Muslims, Christians and Jews living together — modern scholars, like Richard Fletcher (Moorish Spain), say that this is true, and also not fully true. That Ibn Rushd and Maimonides were in Cordoba rests on evidence — but the standing of dhimmis, the jizya, and the harshness of the Almohad time also rest on evidence. In this book both things are recorded in their own notes — and the book has not decided whether that time was 'golden' or not.

Granada 1492 and the expulsions

The fall of Granada in 1492, the order expelling the Jews in the same year, and the expulsion of the Muslims in 1609 — this comes from Richard Fletcher (Moorish Spain) and modern scholars. In this book no detail of the fighting is given — only that it happened, and what came after.

Pause and think — In Cordoba, people of three faiths lived together — and learned from one another. But living together had limits too. Is living together enough — or does living together also need equality? And when living together breaks, what is lost — only a city, or something more?

9 · The Shared Threads — The Scholars, the Sufis, the Trade Routes, and the One Quran · · THE SHARED THREADS — THE SCHOLARS, THE SUFIS, THE TRADE ROUTES, AND THE ONE QURAN

Until now we have seen — Persia, Central Asia, India, Southeast Asia, China, Africa, Spain — so many different peoples, so many different languages, so many different foods and clothes. Yet all of them called themselves one ummah — one community. How did that happen? This part asks that very question — what were the threads that bound so many different peoples together?

The first thread was the scholars. A scholar of Spain read the books of Baghdad, a scholar of Baghdad read the books of India, and a scholar of India read the books of Timbuktu. Ibn Battuta (1304–1369) saw this very thing on his journey — he set out from Morocco, and went as far as China — and everywhere he found the same Quran, the same prayer, and the same books. His book, the Rihla, tells this story — how big the world was, and yet how much one it was.

The second thread was the Sufis. The lodges of the Sufis were everywhere — in Ajmer, in Baghdad, in Konya, and in Java. The orders of the Sufis — like the Qadiri and the Naqshbandi — spread from one place to another — and their disciples knew one another. Sufi poetry was sung everywhere too — Rumi's Masnavi was read in Turkey, and in India too.

The third thread was the trade routes. The sea routes — the Indian Ocean — and the land routes — the Silk Road — these were not only roads for goods, they were also roads for news. The news of one port reached another port — and the book of one city reached another city.

And the fourth thread was one Quran. Muslims all over the world read the same Quran — in the same Arabic, in the same way. That tradition speaks of seven ways of reading the Quran — this was told in earlier books too — and there is a small difference between the readings of Hafs and Warsh — but the Quran stayed one. And the hajj — every year, Muslims from all over the world met in Mecca — traders, scholars, Sufis, kings — all together. The hajj was the place where Muslims from all over the world saw one another — and knew that they were not alone.

Ibn Battuta's Rihla — a book of travel, tradition's counts

Ibn Battuta's journey (about 1325–1354) and his book, the Rihla — this comes from Ibn Battuta's own book. That he travelled about seventy-five thousand miles — this is his own count, and modern scholars say it may be greatly exaggerated — but the road of his journey — from Morocco to China — is certain. In this book no count is taken as settled.

The seven ways, and Hafs and Warsh — from the earlier book

The seven ways of reading the Quran, and the difference between the readings of Hafs and Warsh — this was told in full in the fourth book (The Quran and the Hadith) — and here it is only repeated. In this book nothing new has been added.

Pause and think — Ibn Battuta set out from Morocco — and went as far as China — and everywhere he found the same Quran. Can one book bind so great a world together — or is something else needed too — like traders, Sufis and the hajj?

Closing Reflection — One Faith, Many Peoples · · CLOSING REFLECTION — ONE FAITH, MANY PEOPLES

In this book we have seen — the traders, who carried Islam in ships; the Sufis, who reached people's hearts; the scholars, who went in books; Persia, which gave Islam its poetry; Samarkand and Bukhara, which became cities of learning on the Silk Road; India, where Hindu and Muslim alike came to the shrines of the Sufis; Java, where Islam spread without an army; China, where the mosques looked Chinese; Africa, where Mansa Musa went on hajj and Timbuktu held books; and Spain, where people of three faiths lived together — and then Granada fell.

And we have also seen — that Islam did not spread in one way only. In some places an army went, in some places traders went, in some places Sufis went, and in some places books went. And where Islam reached, it did not force its own shape — in Persia it became Persian, in China it became Chinese, in Java it became Javanese, and in India it became Indian.

In the next book we shall see what happened next in India — the story of the Mughals — from Babur to Aurangzeb, and what came after. But first, carry one question with you —

Islam spread from Spain to China — but everywhere it looked different. Is a faith known by its one shape — or by its many shapes? And when one faith lives among so many different peoples, where does its unity come from — from the book, from the hajj, or from the heart?

'The Spread' — one journey, not one story

In this book 'the spread' is not called one story — it is many stories — of trade, of Sufis, of scholars, and of fighting too. Modern scholars, like Marshall Hodgson and Ira Lapidus, say that the spread of Islam did not happen in one way only — and this book has not chosen one way.

Pause and think — What touched you most in this book — the trader's ship, the Sufi's lodge, the blue domes of Samarkand, Mansa Musa's hajj, the books of Timbuktu, or the arches of Cordoba? And why?

Sources · · SOURCES

Al-Tabari's History (Ta'rikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk) — the greatest source of this book; the stories of Persia, Central Asia and Spain are taken from it.

Al-Masudi's Meadows of Gold (Muruj al-Dhahab) — the stories of Persia, Spain and the traders are taken from it.

Ibn Battuta's Rihla — the book of his travels; the stories of Southeast Asia, Africa and the unity of the world are taken from it.

The book of al-Umari — the story of Mansa Musa's hajj (1324) and of the gold in Cairo is taken from it.

Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist — the list of books; the stories of al-Bukhari, al-Tabari and the scholars are taken from it.

Marshall Hodgson, The Venture of Islam (volumes 1, 2 and 3) — on the spread of Islam, Persia, Central Asia and the unity of the world.

Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period — on the slow change in Persia, and the time it took to become a majority.

Ira Lapidus, A History of Islamic Societies — on the spread of Islam, trade, Sufis and scholars.

Richard Eaton, The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier — on the spread of Islam in India, the Sufis and Bengal.

Richard Fletcher, Moorish Spain — on al-Andalus, the convivencia, and the fall of Granada (1492).

Thomas Arnold, The Preaching of Islam — on this very question — that Islam spread by trade, by Sufis and by preaching, not by the sword.

Hugh Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates — on the early stories of Persia, Central Asia and Spain.

Wherever this book says 'tradition says', that thing is taken from the books of al-Tabari, al-Masudi, Ibn Battuta and Ibn al-Nadim — not from the evidence of history. Where something rests on evidence, its name is given in a separate note. Where there are two views, both are recorded in their own notes — and the book has not decided between them.
